content: 1. Detection by Odor: In a study involving participants sensitive to taste and odor, the lowest concentration of a substance that elicited a response was 15 µg/L. 2. Metolachlor: Metolachlor (CAS No. 51218-45-2) is a selective pre-emergence herbicide used on various crops. It can degrade in soil through biodegradation, photodegradation, and volatilization. While it is relatively mobile and can contaminate groundwater under certain conditions, it is more commonly found in surface water. A concentration of 1 µg/L is achievable using granular activated carbon (GAC) treatment. In a one-year study on dogs, high doses of metolachlor led to reduced kidney weight. In two-year studies on rodents, toxicological effects included reduced body weight gain and food consumption at high doses. There is no evidence of carcinogenicity in mice, but in rats, liver tumors in females and nasal tumors in males were observed. Metolachlor is not genotoxic. 3. Microcystins (Cyanobacterial Toxins): Microcystins (MCs) are naturally occurring heptapeptides produced by cyanobacteria, primarily in freshwater environments. Among the over 250 identified MCs, microcystin-LR (MC-LR) is the most common and studied. Limited data suggest MCs may accumulate in some food items. Concentrations in scums can reach mg/L levels, but outside scum areas, they rarely exceed tens of µg/L. MCs are hepatotoxins, actively transported into cells by organic anion transport proteins (OATPs), with the liver being the primary target. Acute effects include intrahepatic hemorrhage, while chronic effects involve impaired tumor cell proliferation control. Cases of liver damage and fatalities have been reported due to inadequately treated drinking water or renal dialysis water containing high MC levels. The International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) classified MC-LR as a possible human carcinogen (Group 2B) in 2006. Prevention includes source water management, reducing nutrient loading, and optimizing water treatment processes. 4. Molinate: Molinate (CAS No. 2212-67-1) is a herbicide used to control weeds in rice fields. Groundwater pollution by molinate is limited to specific rice-growing regions. It has low persistence in water and soil, with a half-life of about five days. Based on limited data, molinate does not appear to be carcinogenic or mutagenic in experimental animals. 5. Molybdenum: Molybdenum is a naturally occurring element found in soil and used in steel production, agriculture, and as a lubricant additive. Concentrations in drinking water are typically very low, and a formal guideline value is not deemed necessary. However, a health-based value of 0.07 mg/L has been derived, consistent with molybdenum's essential daily requirement. 6. Monochloroacetic Acid: This compound is formed during water chlorination from organic material. No evidence of carcinogenicity was found in two-year studies on rats and mice. It has shown mixed results in mutagenicity assays and is not classified as carcinogenic by IARC. 7. Monochlorobenzene (MCB): MCB is released into the environment mainly through volatilization during industrial use. It has been detected in surface water, groundwater, and drinking water at low concentrations. MCB is of low acute toxicity, with high doses affecting the liver, kidneys, and hematopoietic system. Limited evidence suggests carcinogenicity in male rats at high doses. MCB is not considered mutagenic, and its concentrations in drinking water are well below levels of health concern. 8. MX (3-Chloro-4-dichloromethyl-5-hydroxy-2(5H)-furanone): MX is formed during water chlorination and has been detected in drinking water at very low concentrations. It is a potent mutagen and has shown tumorigenic responses in rats, leading to its classification as possibly carcinogenic to humans (Group 2B) by IARC. However, its concentrations in drinking water are far below levels of health concern, and a formal guideline value is not proposed. 9. Nickel: Nickel is a naturally occurring element primarily used in stainless steel and alloy production. The guideline value for nickel in drinking water is 70 µg/L, based on reproductive toxicity observed in rats. Conventional water treatment and ion-exchange resins can effectively reduce nickel concentrations. 10. Nitrate and Nitrite: Nitrate (NO3−) is a natural plant nutrient and part of the nitrogen cycle, while nitrite (NO2−) is less stable and forms under reducing conditions. Nitrate contamination in water can result from agricultural activities, wastewater disposal, and oxidation of nitrogenous waste. The guideline values are 50 mg/L for nitrate and 3 mg/L for nitrite, designed to protect against methemoglobinemia and thyroid effects in sensitive populations. Combined nitrate and nitrite levels should not exceed a ratio of 1 when compared to their respective guideline values.
